rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while ensuring strongly retained compounds elute. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the early three-peak cluster responds to slope. This should distinguish slope-sensitive overlaps from pairs that require temperature-driven selectivity changes.

The shallower gradient improved the early cluster but incurred a time penalty. Test higher temperature at the original slope to shift selectivity in that cluster while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

At 60 C only one pair remains below target, with ample time before the 10-minute penalty. A shallower gradient tests whether that pair can reach R ≥ 1.5 while retaining the favorable temperature selectivity.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so further lengthening is unlikely to help. Raise the initial organic fraction one step to test a selectivity shift while monitoring retention and resolution of the early peaks.
Increasing phi0 improved the critical pair while preserving adequate separation elsewhere. Test one more step to seek R ≥ 1.5 for every pair, with the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.
Injection 6 achieved the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method, retaining injection 6 as the benchmark if a critical pair falls below R = 1.5.

The 8-minute gradient narrowly missed both critical-pair targets. Lowering phi1 to 0.85 gives a slope between injections 6 and 7, aiming to restore full resolution with a shorter elution time than injection 6.

Injection 8 is fully resolved but its limiting pair has little margin. Test a one-step temperature decrease to determine whether selectivity can provide more balanced critical-pair resolution before attempting further acceleration.

Return to the more favorable 60 C and raise phi0 one step to seek faster elution while strengthening the previously limiting pair. Monitor the other early separations, which may deteriorate as initial retention decreases.

Test a trimmed, shorter gradient with a slope only slightly steeper than the fully resolved injection 8. The estimated last-peak elution fraction is about 0.62, so phi1 = 0.70 should retain adequate elution strength while probing the speed–resolution boundary.

The faster 60 C gradients are near their resolution limit; injection 11 still has a pair below 1.5 despite its rounded CRF. Test the opposite temperature extreme for a possible elution-order reversal that could offer a different fully resolved operating window.

Return to 60 C and test a shallower gradient at phi0 = 0.20 to recover the early separation lost in injection 10. This explores a potentially more robust fully resolved method; phi1 = 0.65 is above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

The higher starting fraction required a much shallower gradient, so return to phi0 = 0.15. Relative to injection 8, modestly reduce the slope to increase the critical-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test whether a further modest slope reduction improves the limiting pair’s safety margin without a time penalty. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, with sufficient final organic strength for complete elution.

Shorten injection 15’s gradient to recover speed while targeting a slope slightly shallower than the fully resolved injection 8. This should restore the marginal separation seen in injection 11 while completing the programmed gradient in six minutes.

Match injection 8’s successful slope but end the gradient earlier to test a lower-organic, shorter programmed gradient. The early critical pairs should retain their resolution; the main question is whether the final hold still elutes the last compound within 10 minutes.

Shorten the fully resolved higher-phi0 method from injection 13 while keeping its gradient slope nearly unchanged. This tests whether that alternative can retain full resolution with a six-minute gradient and sufficient final elution strength.

Probe the remaining grid step between the fastest fully resolved method, injection 8, and the faster but under-resolved injection 7. This directly tests whether elution can be accelerated while preserving R ≥ 1.5 for both critical pairs.

Injection 19 confirms that steepening beyond injection 8 sacrifices the limiting pair. Back off to a slightly shallower, untested gradient to gain resolution margin while targeting faster elution than injection 14.

The maximum CRF is secured, and injection 8 remains the fastest fully resolved method. Test a shallower gradient at the successful starting composition to seek a larger resolution margin while keeping the predicted last peak below 10 minutes.

Match injection 21’s slope at the higher starting organic fraction to seek more balanced critical-pair resolution and earlier final elution. Injection 13 suggests this modest slope reduction should strengthen its limiting pair while preserving the maximum CRF.

Refine between injections 14 and 15 to target a minimum resolution near 1.6 with less retention time than injection 15. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this tests a nearby option with more resolution margin.

Preserve injection 14’s fully resolved slope while shortening the programmed gradient to six minutes. The last peak should elute near the gradient-to-hold transition, testing a compact method with more resolution margin than injection 8.

Use the final injection to test a nearby method expected to retain maximum CRF with a larger critical-pair margin than injection 8 and last elution near 7 minutes. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed method with every pair at R ≥ 1.5.
